hub_intro_html:
Hanford sits at the working center of Kings County — the county seat, the courthouse town, and the crossroads where Highway 198 meets Highway 43. It is also one of the hardest places in California to own a flat roof. Summer afternoons push air temperatures past 100°F for weeks at a stretch, and the membrane or metal panel on top of a packing house can run 150°F or hotter under direct San Joaquin Valley sun. Winter flips the script: tule fog settles over Kings County for days, holding moisture against every seam, fastener, and flashing on a low-slope roof. Add the wind-blown dust that drifts off surrounding row crops, dairies, and open ground, and you have a climate that grinds down conventional roofing from two directions at once — ultraviolet attack in summer, trapped condensation in winter, and abrasive grit all year long.

Allstate Spray Foam & Roofing has spent more than twenty years building and restoring roofs in exactly this climate. We are a family-owned company, fully licensed (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited, and a member of the Spray Polyurethane Foam Alliance. Our crews dispatch from our Tulare County shop, about 35 minutes east of Hanford — a straight run west on CA-198 past Armona and into town. That proximity matters. The building stock around Hanford tells you why spray polyurethane foam and silicone coatings fit here so well. Those facilities are dominated by big, simple, low-slope and metal-panel roofs — thousands of squares of surface that either leak or don't, insulate or don't, and directly affect what it costs to keep product cold and crews comfortable. Closer to Courthouse Square and China Alley, Hanford's civic and institutional buildings — county offices, schools, clinics, churches — carry the same flat-roof burdens on older bones. Our four core services map directly onto that stock. Foam and flat roof repair handles the leaks, ponding, split seams, and storm damage that Kings County winters expose. And commercial spray foam insulation brings closed-cell performance to the metal shops, warehouses, and processing spaces where conditioned air currently pours through un-insulated steel skin.

Every project in Hanford starts the same way: a free assessment. We put a drone over the roof, take core samples where the story underneath needs verifying, and hand you a written bid within 48 hours. No pressure sequence, no mystery-meat pricing — a documented scope with numbers you can compare. New SPF systems typically run $4–$8 per square foot; recoats run $2–$4. We serve all of Kings County from Hanford outward: Lemoore and its commercial corridor along 198, Corcoran and its cotton and processing facilities down Highway 43, Avenal out toward the I-5 corridor, plus Armona, Home Garden, and the unincorporated ag operations in between. spray-foam-roofing.body_html:
Spray Foam Roofing in Hanford: Built for Kings County's Working Roofs

Spray foam roofing in Hanford solves a problem that conventional roofing keeps failing at: keeping a big, flat, sun-hammered Kings County roof watertight and insulated at the same time, for decades, without seams. Hanford is the county seat and the commercial hub of a county that runs on agriculture — dairy processing, tomato and vegetable packing, cotton moving up and down Highway 43, cold storage, and the distribution buildings that feed all of it along the CA-198 corridor. Nearly every one of those operations sits under a low-slope or metal-panel roof, and nearly every one of those roofs is fighting the same three enemies: relentless summer ultraviolet, winter tule fog that holds moisture against every seam for days, and wind-blown ag dust that abrades surfaces and clogs drains.

Spray polyurethane foam — SPF — answers all three at once. Applied as a liquid that expands and cures into a rigid, closed-cell layer, it forms a single monolithic surface across the entire roof: no seams to split, no fasteners to back out, no laps for fog-season moisture to wick into. It bonds directly to the substrate, insulates at roughly R-6.5 per inch, and gets finished with a protective coating that turns the whole assembly into a renewable system. Our family-owned crews have been installing it across the South Valley for more than twenty years, and Hanford is a routine dispatch — about 35 minutes west of our Tulare County shop, straight out CA-198.

What SPF Actually Is — and Why It Behaves Differently

Most roofing is manufactured somewhere else and assembled on your roof: membranes seamed together, panels screwed down, plies mopped in overlapping courses. Every joint in that assembly is a future maintenance item. Spray polyurethane foam roofing is manufactured on your roof. Two liquid components meet at the spray gun, react in seconds, and expand roughly thirty-fold into rigid foam that welds itself to the deck and to every previous pass. The result is one continuous piece of roofing, custom-fit to your building's exact geometry.

That changes how the roof handles the details that leak first. Penetrations — pipes, curbs, HVAC stands, skylight frames, the conduit runs that ag processing equipment always seems to sprout — get foamed in place, self-flashed by the same material as the field of the roof. Parapets and transitions become smooth, sealed coves instead of caulked joints. And because the foam is closed-cell, with a compressive strength in the 40-to-60-psi range for roofing formulations, it resists foot traffic from your own maintenance crews and shrugs off the thermal cycling that tears seamed systems apart.

The finished SPF layer is then armored with an elastomeric topcoat — typically silicone in our climate — that blocks UV and takes the weathering. That coat, not the foam, is the sacrificial layer, which is why the system renews on a recoat cycle instead of a replacement cycle.

A 150°F Roof Deck: The Physics Working Against Hanford Buildings

Kings County summers are not gentle. Air temperatures over 100°F are standard from June into September, and a dark built-up or aged single-ply roof surface in Hanford can run 150°F or hotter by mid-afternoon. At those temperatures, asphaltic materials cook — plasticizers migrate out, surfaces alligator, and every degree of extra heat drives the building's cooling equipment harder. Then, sometime after Thanksgiving, the tule fog arrives. Kings County sits low in the basin, and fog can hold at saturation for days at a time, feeding moisture into every lap, blister, and fastener hole that summer opened up.

An SPF roof with a bright white silicone topcoat inverts the summer half of that cycle. High-reflectivity coatings bounce the majority of solar radiation before it ever becomes heat in the assembly, dropping peak surface temperatures dramatically compared to dark membranes. The foam beneath then insulates the deck from what heat remains, at R-6.5 per inch, continuously, with no thermal bridging through fasteners — because there are no fasteners. In fog season, the seamless surface gives condensation and wind-driven moisture nowhere to enter. The same closed-cell structure that insulates also refuses to wick water laterally, which is why a properly maintained SPF roof handles Hanford's wet-winter, brutal-summer swing better than anything assembled from parts.

Dust matters here too. Wind off the surrounding row crops and open ground loads Hanford roofs with fine grit that abrades coatings and dams up drainage on dead-flat decks. SPF lets us rebuild slope where a roof has none — foam can be applied thicker in low areas to re-establish positive drainage toward existing drains and scuppers, turning a chronic ponding roof into one that actually sheds water.

Commercial Roofing Hanford Operations Can Stop Rebuying

For commercial roofing, Hanford building owners have usually been through the cycle at least once: patch the built-up roof, patch it again, re-membrane, watch the new seams start failing within a decade, repeat. SPF breaks the cycle for a simple reason — in most cases it installs directly over the existing roof after inspection, cleaning, and preparation. That means no tear-off, which means no days with your packing line or county office open to the sky, no dumpsters of old roofing hauled to the landfill, and no gamble on weather mid-project.

For Hanford's commercial mix, that translates specifically:

  • Ag processing and packing plants — production can't stop for a tear-off, and SPF installation is staged section by section over an operating facility.
  • Cold storage and distribution — every point of R-value on the roof shows up directly on the refrigeration bill; SPF adds insulation and waterproofing in the same pass.
  • Civic and institutional buildings — as the county seat, Hanford carries courthouses-era downtown stock, county offices, schools, and clinics whose older flat roofs need renewal without structural surprises; foam is lightweight, typically under a pound per square foot for a standard application.
  • Retail and service buildings along Lacey Boulevard and the 198 corridor — where a leak over inventory or a patient waiting room is a business interruption, not just a maintenance ticket.

We are fully licensed (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited, and an SPFA member — and because our crews dispatch from Tulare County, follow-up service in Hanford is a half-hour drive, not a scheduling negotiation.

Metal Building Roofing: SPF Over Steel Panels

Drive any industrial street in Hanford, or out Highway 43 toward the gins and processing yards, and you're looking at metal buildings — pre-engineered steel, R-panel and standing seam roofs, decades of them. Metal building roofing fails in predictable ways here: fastener gaskets dry out and back out under thermal cycling, panel laps open up, rust blooms where dust and fog-season condensation sit, and the un-insulated or minimally insulated interior becomes an oven by July.

SPF over metal is one of the strongest applications in the entire spray foam playbook. The foam locks down the panels and fasteners under a continuous rigid layer, ending the daily expansion-contraction movement that works screws loose. It seals every lap and penetration permanently. It adds real insulation — R-13 in two inches, R-19 in three — directly to the underside of the sun. And it quiets the building; the drumming of wind and the pop and tick of metal moving through a 60-degree daily temperature swing largely disappear under foam.

Condensation is the quiet killer of Valley metal buildings, and it's worth its own paragraph. In fog season, a bare steel roof panel cools to the fog temperature while interior air holds moisture from washdown operations, propane heaters, or simple occupancy — and the underside of the panel rains. On buildings storing ag equipment, packaged product, or hay, that drip does real damage. Closed-cell foam on the panel keeps the steel's interior surface at conditioned-space temperature, which means it never hits the dew point, which means the raining stops. We treat roof-side SPF and interior-side insulation as complementary tools — see our commercial insulation service for the interior half of that equation.

Flat and Low-Slope Roofs on Processing and Packing Facilities

Kings County's processing stock — dairy and cheese operations, tomato packers, nut and vegetable handlers — runs on large, flat or nearly flat roofs crowded with equipment. Those roofs are hard duty: refrigeration curbs and condensate lines, exhaust penetrations, catwalks, and steam or washdown moisture from below. Every piece of rooftop equipment on a seamed membrane roof is a ring of flashing waiting to fail.

SPF was practically designed for this. Foam flows around curbs, stands, and penetrations and seals them as part of the roof field itself. Where equipment vibrates, foam's adhesion and rigidity resist the working-loose that kills pitch pans and term bars. Where washdown steam loads the deck from below, closed-cell foam refuses to absorb it. And where USDA-adjacent cleanliness standards make interior leak staining a compliance issue rather than a cosmetic one, a seamless roof is the difference between an audit note and a clean walk-through.

Scheduling is the other half. Processing runs on harvest calendars — tomato season doesn't pause because a roofer is booked. Because SPF is spray-applied in sections with same-day waterproofing as each area is coated, we stage installations around production: block by block, weekend windows where needed, no long stretches of exposed deck. The installation process is engineered around occupied, operating buildings.

R-6.5 Per Inch, Title 24, and the Cooling-Load Math

California's Title 24 energy code pushes commercial roofing toward two things: cool-roof surfaces and continuous insulation. SPF with a reflective silicone topcoat delivers both in one system. The foam itself installs at roughly R-6.5 per inch — among the highest R-values per inch of any field-applied insulation — and because it's continuous across the deck, its installed performance isn't degraded by the fastener and joint bridging that undercuts board-stock insulation.

Run the Hanford math. A 30,000-square-foot packing or warehouse roof with minimal existing insulation, in a climate with hundred-plus cooling days, is bleeding conditioned air upward all summer. Two to three inches of SPF adds R-13 to R-19 on top of whatever the roof already has, while the white topcoat drops the surface temperature the insulation has to fight. Owners typically see the impact in the first PG&E summer bill; over a multi-year hold it becomes one of the few roofing decisions that pays for part of itself. For buildings pursuing Title 24 compliance during alterations, the SPF assembly's aged reflectance and continuous R-value make documentation straightforward.

What Spray Foam Roofing Costs in Hanford

Spray foam roofing costs in Hanford follow the same honest ranges we quote everywhere in the Valley: new SPF systems typically run $4–$8 per square foot depending on foam thickness, substrate preparation, tear-off avoidance, and roof complexity; recoating an existing foam roof runs $2–$4 per square foot. The pattern that matters: SPF's lifecycle cost bends downward because the expensive event — tear-off and re-install — ideally never recurs. A full breakdown of what drives pricing up or down is on our spray foam roofing cost page. Every Hanford bid we write is preceded by a free assessment — drone survey, core sampling where the existing assembly needs verification, and a written bid in your hands within 48 hours.

How Installation Works From Our Tulare County Shop

Our crews stage out of Tulare County and reach Hanford in about 35 minutes via CA-198 — close enough that mobilization doesn't distort the bid and follow-up doesn't fall off the calendar. A typical Hanford SPF project runs:

  • Assessment. Drone survey of the entire roof field, core samples where the existing assembly or suspected saturation needs verification, moisture mapping on problem roofs. Written bid within 48 hours.
  • Preparation. Cleaning and drying of the substrate, removal of saturated sections only (not blanket tear-off), priming as the substrate requires, masking and wind screens to protect neighboring property — a discipline we take seriously in tight downtown blocks near Courthouse Square.
  • Foam application. SPF applied in controlled passes to the specified thickness, building slope-to-drain where the deck needs it. Each day's area is weathered-in before the crew leaves.
  • Topcoat and granules. Silicone coating applied at specified millage over the cured foam, with embedded granules where foot traffic or hail resistance calls for them.
  • Documentation. Final drone imagery, coating thickness records, and the maintenance schedule that keeps the recoat cycle — and our industry-leading leak-proof guarantees — intact.

Weather windows matter in Kings County: foam wants a dry substrate and reasonable wind, so we schedule around fog-season saturation and afternoon dust events. That's local knowledge, and it's the difference between an SPF roof that lasts decades and one that blisters in year two.

SPF vs. TPO and the Other Options for Kings County

Owners comparing systems usually shortlist SPF against TPO single-ply, and the honest answer is that both are legitimate roofs — the question is which failure modes your building can live with. TPO is factory-consistent sheet membrane with heat-welded seams; its weak points are exactly those seams, its fastener rows, and its flashing details, all of which multiply on equipment-crowded ag roofs. SPF has no seams, self-flashes every penetration, and adds insulation TPO doesn't — but demands a properly prepared substrate and an experienced applicator. Our full side-by-side is at spray foam vs. TPO roofing.

In Hanford specifically, three local factors tilt the comparison. First, equipment density: packing and processing roofs have too many penetrations for seamed systems to protect economically. Second, the thermal swing: 150°F summer decks and 35°F fog nights work seams and fasteners relentlessly, while a monolithic foam layer moves as one piece. Third, dust: grit abrades single-ply surfaces and finds every mechanical joint, while a coated foam roof presents one smooth, renewable surface. For dead-flat roofs with chronic ponding, SPF's ability to rebuild slope is frequently the deciding factor all by itself.

Serving Lemoore, Corcoran, Avenal, and All of Kings County

Hanford is the hub, but the same crews cover the whole county. In Lemoore, ten minutes west on 198, we roof the commercial corridor that serves the naval air station community — the medical offices, shops, restaurants, and service businesses that town supports — along with its ag processing base. In Corcoran, down Highway 43, the building stock runs to cotton gins, grain and processing structures, and institutional flat roofs, all of it under the same sun and dust load as Hanford. Avenal, out toward the I-5 corridor on the county's west side, adds oil-country and institutional buildings to the mix. Armona, Home Garden, Stratford, and Kettleman City fall inside the same service radius.

Distance never changes the process: free drone assessment, core sampling where warranted, written bid in 48 hours, and a crew that's based one county over rather than three hours up Highway 99.

The Long Game: A Recoat Cycle Instead of a Tear-Off Cycle

The most important number in this entire page might be this one: 10 to 20 years. That's the recoat cycle of a properly installed SPF roof — the interval at which the sacrificial silicone topcoat gets cleaned, inspected, and re-applied at $2–$4 per square foot. The foam beneath, protected from UV, doesn't age out; industry experience with SPF roofs now runs past four decades on systems that were simply recoated on schedule. The full story on longevity is at how long does spray foam roofing last.

For a Hanford building owner, that reframes the roof from a recurring capital emergency into a predictable maintenance line. No more budgeting a six-figure tear-off every fifteen years; no more gambling on whether the next membrane outlives the next drought cycle. One system, renewed on schedule, backed by industry-leading leak-proof guarantees and a family-owned company that has been doing exactly this work in the South Valley for more than twenty years.

silicone-roof-coating.body_html:
Silicone Roof Coating in Hanford: Restoration Instead of Replacement

Silicone roof coating gives Hanford building owners a way out of the most expensive sentence in commercial property ownership: "the roof needs to be replaced." In most cases, it doesn't. If the deck is sound and the existing roof — foam, built-up, modified bitumen, single-ply, or metal — is aging rather than structurally failed, a fluid-applied 100% silicone system restores it to watertight, reflective, warrantable condition for $2–$4 per square foot instead of the $5–$12 that tear-off and re-roofing runs. For the packing houses, warehouses, county buildings, and Highway 198 corridor businesses that make up Hanford's commercial stock, that difference is frequently six figures.

The logic is simple: most "failed" roofs in Kings County aren't failed structures, they're failed surfaces. Twenty summers of Valley sun cooks the top layer — asphalt alligators, membranes chalk, coatings thin out — while the assembly underneath is still doing its job. Silicone replaces that spent surface with a seamless, UV-immune, ponding-proof skin that bonds to what's there and weathers in its place. It's the same chemistry we use as the protective topcoat on our spray foam roofs, applied here as a restoration system in its own right. Family-owned, licensed (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited, SPFA member, and 35 minutes from Hanford via CA-198 — we've been coating South Valley roofs for more than twenty years.

What "100% Silicone" Actually Means

Coatings are not interchangeable, and the label matters. We install high-solids, 100% silicone coatings — meaning the wet film you pay for cures into nearly the same thickness of dry rubber, rather than losing a third of its volume to evaporating carriers. Compare that with economy acrylics, which are water-based: they lose significant film build as they dry, they re-soften under standing water, and they wear measurably every year under UV and dust scour.

Silicone's chemistry is inorganic at its backbone, which is why the San Joaquin Valley's most punishing input — ultraviolet radiation — essentially doesn't age it. It stays flexible from freezing fog mornings to 150°F afternoon decks. It is moisture-cure, meaning humidity helps rather than hinders curing. And critically for Kings County's dead-flat roofs, it is unaffected by ponding water: where acrylics blister and re-emulsify under a week-long winter pond, silicone simply doesn't care. When we say the words "100% silicone" in a Hanford bid, that's the entire performance story in three words.

Why Roof Coating Makes Sense for Kings County Buildings

Roof coating in Hanford earns its keep on three local realities. First, the economics of big simple roofs: ag processing plants, cold storage, gins, and distribution buildings carry enormous square footage, so the per-foot spread between coating and replacing multiplies fast. A 40,000-square-foot warehouse roof coated at $3 per square foot versus replaced at $8 is a $200,000 decision.

Second, business continuity. Coating is a low-disruption process — no tear-off, no exposed deck, no dumpster convoys, minimal noise. Packing lines keep running, county offices stay open, clinic waiting rooms stay quiet. On food-adjacent facilities where an open roof is a contamination risk, restoration versus replacement isn't just cheaper; it's operationally safer.

Third, the energy math. A fresh white silicone surface reflects the large majority of solar energy that a gray, weathered roof was absorbing. In a town with a hundred-plus days of cooling load, dropping the roof surface temperature by 50 degrees or more shows up on the PG&E bill the very first summer, and it helps alteration projects pencil under California's Title 24 cool-roof provisions without redesigning the assembly.

Silicone Flat Roof Coating and the Ponding Problem

Hanford was laid out on some of the flattest ground in California, and its roofs match the terrain. Dead-flat decks plus winter rain plus tule fog that slows evaporation for days equals ponding — the standing water that kills more Valley flat roofs than any other single cause. Water sitting on a seamed membrane finds the laps. Water sitting on aged asphalt soaks into the alligatoring. Water sitting on a clogged drain field freezes on fog-season nights and pries surfaces apart.

Silicone flat roof coating is the only major coating chemistry that's flatly warrantable under permanent ponding. It doesn't re-emulsify, doesn't blister from moisture drive, and doesn't lose adhesion under standing water. On chronic-pond roofs we go further: because we're also a spray foam company, we can build foam crickets and slope corrections in the low spots before coating, converting a birdbath deck into one that drains. That combination — spray polyurethane foam for geometry, silicone for surface — is a fix that a coatings-only contractor simply can't offer.

Wind-blown ag dust makes ponding worse than the rainfall numbers suggest. Grit washes to the low spots and drains, forms dams, and deepens the ponds year over year. Our maintenance schedules for Hanford roofs include drain-field checks timed to the post-harvest dust season, because a coating system is only as good as the drainage it sits on.

Silicone roof coating costs in Hanford run $2–$4 per square foot for a typical restoration, with position inside that range driven by the variables below:

Cost DriverPushes Toward $2/sq ftPushes Toward $4/sq ft
Existing surfaceSound SPF or smooth single-ply needing standard prepGranulated mod-bit or rusted metal needing heavy prep/primer
Moisture in assemblyDry cores, clean infrared scanSaturated areas requiring cut-out and foam repair first
Roof complexityOpen field, few penetrationsEquipment-crowded processing roof, many details to flash
Specified millageStandard restoration buildHigh-build system for maximum warranty term
Access & stagingSingle-story, open yardTight downtown block near Courthouse Square, limited staging

Compare any number in that range against replacement and the argument usually ends there — but the honest comparison includes the roof's condition. Coating a roof that's too far gone wastes money, which is why every Hanford project starts with a free assessment: drone survey of the whole field, core samples where the assembly's story needs verifying, and a written bid within 48 hours. If what your roof actually needs is repair first, or full SPF, the bid says so — with numbers from our spray foam roofing cost guide so you can weigh both paths.

The Pros and Cons of Silicone — Straight Answers

Every material has trade-offs, and you should hear silicone's from the people who install it. The pros, concentrated:

  • UV immunity. Valley sun doesn't meaningfully degrade silicone — the single most important property on a 150°F Hanford roof.
  • Ponding resistance. Warrantable under standing water; the decisive advantage on Kings County's dead-flat decks.
  • Seamless application. Fluid-applied, it flashes penetrations and details as part of the field.
  • Renewability. When the coating wears, you clean and recoat — the roof never goes back to zero.
  • Reflectivity. High solar reflectance cuts cooling loads and supports Title 24 compliance.

And the cons, stated plainly:

  • Slick when wet. Cured silicone is slippery in rain or fog; we embed granules in walkway paths and around equipment on roofs with regular foot traffic.
  • Dust pickup. Fresh silicone holds airborne dust more than some surfaces — real in Hanford's ag environment. It dulls the bright white over time, which is cosmetic, and periodic cleaning restores most reflectivity.
  • Recoat loyalty. Almost nothing adheres to silicone except more silicone — a non-issue if you maintain the system, a constraint if you later want a different chemistry.
  • Not a structural fix. Coating restores surfaces; it cannot rescue a saturated or structurally failed roof. Honest assessment has to come first, and ours does.

Metal Roof Coating for Ag and Industrial Steel

Metal roof coating may be the highest-return version of this entire service in Kings County, because the county is carpeted in steel: pre-engineered shops and warehouses in Hanford's industrial blocks, gin and processing structures down Highway 43 toward Corcoran, equipment barns on every section of farmland, and the commercial steel that serves Lemoore and Avenal. Metal roofs here fail at their details — fastener gaskets baked dead by decade two, panel laps opened by thermal cycling, rust tracking along seams where fog condensation sits — long before the panels themselves are done.

Our metal restoration sequence attacks exactly those details: pressure wash and prep, rust conversion on oxidized areas, seam and fastener treatment — every screw head individually encapsulated or brush-sealed — then a full-field 100% silicone application at specified millage. The result is a monolithic waterproof skin over the entire panel system, reflective white instead of heat-soaking galvanized or faded paint, with every one of the ten thousand fasteners that used to be a future leak sealed under rubber.

Two Hanford-specific notes. First, condensation: coating the exterior doesn't stop interior-side panel sweating in fog season — that's an insulation problem, and our commercial spray foam service handles it from the underside; the two treatments together fully rehabilitate a steel building envelope. Second, heat: an un-coated metal roof radiates brutal heat into shop space all summer, and owners consistently report the workspace itself feels different the first week after a white silicone coat goes on.

Recoating SPF Roofs: The 10–20 Year Cycle

If your building already has a foam roof — and plenty of Kings County ag facilities do — silicone recoating is the maintenance act that makes it permanent. SPF roofs age from the topcoat down: the silicone weathers slowly, thinning over 10–20 years, while the foam beneath stays protected. Recoat before the foam is ever exposed and the cycle resets; the system's documented lifespan then extends past four decades, as covered in how long does spray foam roofing last.

Our recoat process on foam: clean, inspect the entire field, repair any impact damage or blisters — the fix procedures live on our foam roof repair page — then re-apply silicone to full specified thickness. At $2–$4 per square foot on a 10-to-20-year interval, it's among the cheapest per-year roofing costs any commercial building can achieve. We put every Hanford foam roof we touch on a documented recoat schedule so the interval is tracked by us, not by whoever notices a leak first.

Fog, Dust, and 150°F: The Local Conditions That Choose the Coating

Material selection is climate-driven, and Kings County's climate makes the choice unusually clear-cut. Summer delivers months of extreme UV and roof surfaces at 150°F — conditions that age organic coatings fast and favor silicone's inorganic backbone. Winter delivers tule fog: near-permanent surface moisture for days at a stretch, which punishes water-sensitive acrylics during both application windows and service life, while moisture-cure silicone is unbothered. The dust load off surrounding fields scours all surfaces, favoring high-build systems with granule reinforcement in traffic areas. And the daily thermal swing — a fog-chilled morning to a blistering afternoon — demands the elasticity silicone keeps across that whole range.

This is also why application timing is a local skill. We schedule Hanford coating work around fog-season dew points and afternoon wind events, verify substrate moisture before spraying, and adjust cure windows to the season. A coating spec written for San Diego fails in the basin; ours are written for the basin.

From Drone Survey to Final Millage: How We Work

Every silicone project in Hanford follows the same documented arc. The free assessment comes first: drone survey of the full roof field, core sampling where saturation is suspected, and a written bid within 48 hours that states plainly whether your roof is a coating candidate, a repair-then-coat candidate, or past restoring. Preparation follows — wash-down, moisture cut-outs and foam repairs, rust conversion on metal, primer where the substrate chemistry requires it. Application is measured, not eyeballed: silicone goes down at specified wet millage, verified with gauges, with details and penetrations brush-flashed before the field coat ties everything together. Granules are embedded in walkways and around serviced equipment. Final documentation includes drone imagery, thickness records, and the maintenance schedule that keeps our industry-leading leak-proof guarantees in force.

That paper trail matters more than it sounds. Kings County buildings change hands, managers rotate, and ten years from now somebody will want to know what's on this roof and when it's due. Our documentation answers that question — and because we're 35 minutes away, the company that installed it is still the company that services it.

Lemoore, Corcoran, Avenal — County-Wide Coverage

The crews that coat Hanford roofs cover all of Kings County on the same terms. Lemoore's commercial corridor — the retail, dining, medical, and service businesses sustained by the naval air station community — plus its dairy and processing operations sit ten minutes west on 198. Corcoran's gins, grain structures, and institutional buildings are a straight run down Highway 43. Avenal anchors the county's west side out toward Interstate 5, with institutional and commercial stock that bakes under the same sun. Armona, Home Garden, Stratford, and Kettleman City all fall inside the normal dispatch radius from our Tulare County shop.

If your flat, foam, or metal roof anywhere in that footprint is showing its age — chalking, alligatoring, rust tracks, ponding rings, or the first interior stains — the assessment that tells you whether $3 a foot can save it is free. Call (559) 739-9519 and we'll schedule the drone.

Roof Repair in Hanford: Flat, Foam, and Low-Slope Specialists

Roof repair in Hanford is mostly flat-roof repair, whether the listings admit it or not. The county seat's commercial blocks, its packing and processing facilities, its schools and county buildings, and the metal shops lining Highway 43 all run on low-slope and flat assemblies — and when they leak, they leak in ways that pitched-roof contractors routinely misdiagnose. Water on a flat roof travels: it enters at a split seam near the HVAC curb, runs forty feet along the deck flutes, and drips into a hallway nowhere near the actual breach. Fixing the stain instead of the source is how Hanford buildings end up with five patches and the same leak.

We approach it differently because flat, foam, and low-slope roofs are all we do. Allstate Spray Foam & Roofing is family-owned, more than twenty years in the South Valley, fully licensed (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited, and an SPFA member. Our crews reach Hanford in about 35 minutes from our Tulare County shop, straight out CA-198 — close enough that a repair call doesn't sit in a queue behind a week of drive-time excuses. Every repair starts with actual diagnosis: drone survey of the full roof field, core sampling where the assembly's condition is in question, and a written bid within 48 hours that tells you what's wrong, what it takes to fix it, and what it costs.

How Kings County Weather Breaks Roofs

Hanford's climate attacks roofs on a schedule. Summer is the slow kill: months of 100°F-plus air and roof surfaces near 150°F cook the oils out of asphalt, chalk single-ply membranes, and cycle every seam and fastener through a daily expansion-contraction workout. By September, the roof is brittle, micro-cracked, and primed to fail — but it hasn't rained yet, so nobody knows.

Then winter arrives with the reveal. The first real storms find every seam that summer opened. Tule fog follows and makes it worse in a way outsiders underestimate: fog holds the roof surface at saturation for days at a time, giving water a standing invitation to wick into laps, blisters, and fastener holes that a brief rain would have run past. Freeze-adjacent fog nights pry openings wider. Meanwhile, wind-blown dust off the surrounding ag ground has spent the whole year washing into drains and low spots, damming water into ponds that sit exactly where the membrane is weakest.

That cycle — summer embrittlement, autumn dust load, winter saturation — is why Hanford roof leaks cluster in the first storms of the season, and why the smartest repair call is the one made in October, before the ceiling tile stains.

Finding the Leak: Drone Survey and Core Sampling

Diagnosis is the half of leak repair that most repair outfits skip. Ours is systematic. The drone survey covers the entire roof field in high resolution — not just the area over the drip — because flat-roof water travel means the entry point is frequently a long way from the symptom. We're looking for the full catalog: open seams, split flashings, crushed foam around equipment stands, ponding rings, clogged drains and scuppers, fastener back-out patterns on metal, blistering on built-up surfaces.

Where the surface story is ambiguous, core sampling settles it. A core tells us what the assembly actually is — Hanford's older downtown buildings near Courthouse Square routinely carry three generations of roofing stacked up — and whether the insulation is wet. That distinction drives everything: a dry assembly with a local breach is a repair; a saturated field is a different conversation, honestly had. Moisture that stays trapped under a cosmetic patch doesn't just persist — it corrodes decks, grows mold, destroys R-value, and turns a four-figure repair into a six-figure replacement a few years out.

Everything we find goes into a written bid within 48 hours: photos, findings, scope, and numbers. No mystery, no verbal drift, no "while we're up here" surprises.

Flat Roof Repair Across Built-Up, Modified, and Single-Ply Systems

Flat roof repair in Hanford means being fluent in every system the last sixty years installed. Built-up gravel roofs on older civic and commercial buildings fail by alligatoring, blistering, and flashing splits at parapets — we repair with compatible plies and mastics, then talk honestly about whether a silicone restoration should follow. Modified bitumen fails at end laps and around whatever equipment was added after the roof went on — repairs are torch-or-cold-applied to match the system. Single-ply TPO and EPDM fail at seams, punctures, and shrinkage-stressed corners — we heat-weld or seam-repair with manufacturer-matched materials rather than smearing caulk over a membrane problem.

The pattern across all three: match the repair to the system, fix the detail that failed, and never bury moisture. Mismatched patch materials are their own failure mode — asphalt products attacking single-ply chemistry, incompatible mastics letting go in the first hot week — and Hanford roofs are full of them. Bringing in a crew that actually stocks and knows the right materials is the difference between a repair and a delay.

Foam Roof Repair: Blisters, Bird Pecks, and Impact Damage

Foam roof repair is our home turf — we install SPF, so we repair it with the fluency of the people who build it. SPF roofs in Kings County are tough, but they take damage in recognizable ways: impact gouges from dropped tools or wind-flung debris, bird pecking (a real Valley phenomenon, especially near ag operations where birds work the roofline), blisters where a past applicator sprayed over damp substrate, and topcoat wear-through on roofs that missed their recoat window.

The repairs are straightforward when done right: cut out damaged or wet foam back to sound material, dry the area, re-foam to grade, and re-coat with silicone tied into the surrounding field. Small punctures get sealant-and-mesh treatment; larger areas get the full cut-and-refoam. What kills foam roofs isn't damage — it's neglected damage, because exposed foam ages under UV. Caught early, a foam repair is one of the cheapest fixes in commercial roofing; our complete procedures are documented on the foam roof repair page. Kept on a recoat schedule afterward, the roof's lifespan keeps extending — see how long does spray foam roofing last for what that curve looks like over decades.

Leak Repair That Ends at the Cause, Not the Symptom

Leak repair earns its name only when the water stops for good, and that requires refusing two temptations. The first is patching the stain: tracing interior drips to the actual breach takes drone imagery, moisture logic, and sometimes cores — but a patch over the wrong spot is money spent to keep leaking. The second is patching over saturation: if the insulation around a breach is wet, sealing the top traps the problem in the assembly, where it quietly destroys the deck and R-value until the roof fails wholesale.

Our leak repairs in Hanford therefore always include the boring parts: verifying the entry point, checking the moisture halo around it, drying or removing wet material, and repairing with system-matched materials at the detail that failed — seam, flashing, penetration boot, pitch pan, drain bowl, or field breach. Then we document what we did and photograph it, because the next manager of that building deserves to know what's under the surface. It's the difference between a company that sells patches and a company that ends leaks.

Ponding Water: The Repair That's Really a Drainage Fix

Ponding is Hanford's signature roof disease. The town is table-flat, the roofs were built to match, and decades of settling plus dust accumulation leave most older flat roofs with birdbaths that hold water for days after rain — or weeks in fog season, when evaporation nearly stops. Standing water accelerates every failure mode: it soaks into aged asphalt, works seams, breeds algae that holds moisture even longer, and concentrates load on the deck's weakest framing.

Treating ponding as a leak problem misses the point; it's a geometry problem. Our fix menu runs from cheap to structural: clearing and rebuilding drain fields and scuppers that ag dust has dammed; installing overflow paths where original drainage was underbuilt; and — the tool most repair contractors don't have — spraying polyurethane foam crickets and slope build-ups that reshape the deck so water moves to the drains. Because spray polyurethane foam is fully adhered and self-flashing, it re-slopes a roof without the dead-load and cost of tapered board systems. Coated in silicone, the corrected areas are also the most waterproof parts of the roof.

What Your Roof Is Telling You

Most Hanford roof failures announce themselves months before the ceiling stain. Here's the translation table:

Symptom You SeeLikely CauseRight Repair
Ceiling stain after first fall rainSummer-opened seam or flashing, water traveling on deckTrace to entry, system-matched seam/flashing repair
Dark rings on the roof surfaceChronic ponding from settling or dammed drainsDrain rebuild + foam slope correction
Bubbles or spongy areas underfootBlistering / trapped moisture in assemblyCore sample, cut-and-dry or cut-and-refoam
Rust streaks below fastener rows (metal)Backed-out fasteners, dead gasketsFastener re-secure + seal, or coating-grade restoration
Exposed yellow/orange foamSPF topcoat worn through, UV eating foamLocal re-foam + silicone recoat before it spreads
Granules or membrane chalk in guttersSurface aging into failure phaseRepair now + restoration conversation

If any row of that table describes your building, the assessment that confirms it is free.

When You Need Us Fast — and What We Honestly Promise

Storm damage doesn't schedule itself, and when a winter system rips flashing off a Hanford packing house at the wrong moment, speed matters. Here is our honest commitment: we're 35 minutes away, we prioritize active-leak calls, and we'll tell you on the phone what temporary measures to take before we arrive. What we won't do is invent a guaranteed response-time SLA for marketing purposes — anyone quoting you "emergency crews standing by 24/7" in a county this size deserves skepticism.

What we can genuinely deliver is triage that works: emergency dry-in measures to stop active water entry, honest same-visit assessment of whether the fix is immediate or needs materials, and the full documented repair right behind it. For operations where roof failure means product loss — cold storage, packed inventory, records storage in county buildings — we also strongly recommend the preventive route: a pre-season inspection each fall costs almost nothing against one pallet of water-damaged product.

Repair, Restore, or Replace: The Honest Decision Tree

Not every damaged roof should be repaired — and not every aging roof should be replaced. The decision logic we walk Hanford owners through: if damage is local and the assembly is dry, repair — it's the cheapest correct answer, and most calls end here. If the surface is broadly aged but the assembly is sound and dry, restore — a silicone coating system at $2–$4 per square foot resets the roof's clock for a fraction of replacement. If cores show widespread saturation, deck damage, or a roof past its structural life, replace — usually with SPF at $4–$8 per square foot, which installs over the prepared substrate without full tear-off in most cases; the complete economics live on our spray foam roofing cost page.

The point of the free assessment is that you get this decision made with data — drone imagery and core results — instead of with whichever answer the contractor happened to be selling. We install and repair every option on that tree, so we have no incentive to push you up it.

Metal Roof Leak Repair on Shops, Gins, and Warehouses

Kings County's steel buildings deserve their own repair playbook. Metal roof leaks almost never come through the panel; they come through the details — fastener holes where gaskets died in the heat, lap seams that opened under thermal cycling, ridge and eave closures that dust and fog corrosion ate, and rust-through where condensation sat along the purlin lines. Our metal repairs re-secure or replace backed-out fasteners with oversized gasketed screws, seal laps and closures with metal-rated sealants and mesh, convert surface rust before it perforates, and — where the detail failures are roof-wide — quote the honest upgrade: a full silicone restoration that seals every fastener and lap under one monolithic coat, or SPF over the panels for insulation and waterproofing in one pass.

Fog-season condensation drip inside metal buildings gets misdiagnosed as leaking constantly. If your "leak" appears on cold clear mornings without rain, it's condensation — an insulation problem, not a breach — and the fix is on our commercial insulation page, not a tube of caulk.

Serving Hanford, Lemoore, Corcoran, and Avenal

Our repair radius covers all of Kings County on the same terms as Hanford proper: Lemoore and the commercial corridor serving the naval air station community, ten minutes west on 198; Corcoran's gins, processing structures, and institutional roofs down Highway 43; Avenal on the county's west side toward I-5; plus Armona, Home Garden, Stratford, and the unincorporated ag operations between them. Same crews, same 48-hour written bids, same materials in the rig.

If your roof is leaking now, staining ceilings, holding ponds, or just overdue for the fall inspection that catches all of the above early — call (559) 739-9519. The drone survey and the diagnosis are free, and the crew is 35 minutes away.

Why does my Hanford flat roof only leak during the first storms of the season?

Because summer does the damage and winter reveals it. Months of 150°F roof surfaces embrittle seams and flashings, then the first real rain — followed by days of tule fog holding the surface at saturation — finds every opening. That's also why a fall inspection is the highest-value repair dollar you can spend in Kings County.
The ceiling stain is nowhere near where you found the hole. How is that possible?

Water on a flat roof travels. It enters at a seam or flashing, runs along the deck — sometimes forty feet or more along metal deck flutes — and drips at the first opening it finds. That's why we drone-survey the entire roof field instead of just patching above the stain, which is how buildings end up with five patches and the same leak.

Probably not — that's fog-season condensation. The bare steel panels cool to fog temperature while interior air holds moisture, and the underside of the roof rains. It's an insulation problem, not a breach, and the durable fix is closed-cell spray foam on the panels rather than sealant on the roof.
Is it worth repairing an old foam roof, or should it be replaced?

Foam roofs are almost always worth repairing — that's one of their core advantages. Damaged or wet foam gets cut out, re-foamed, and re-coated, and the repair becomes part of the monolithic roof. commercial-insulation.body_html:
Commercial Spray Foam Insulation in Hanford: Steel Buildings, Real R-Value

Commercial spray foam insulation in Hanford exists because Kings County built its economy inside metal buildings — and metal buildings, left un-insulated, are thermally honest to a fault. The pre-engineered steel shops, warehouses, gins, packing structures, and equipment barns that line Hanford's industrial blocks and run down Highway 43 toward Corcoran are essentially single-wall steel enclosures: whatever the weather is doing outside, the steel delivers inside within minutes. In a county where summer means months over 100°F and winter means weeks of tule fog, that honesty gets expensive — in cooling bills, in condensation damage, in product loss, and in workspaces that are genuinely brutal by 2 p.m. in July.

Closed-cell spray polyurethane foam is the definitive fix for steel-skinned commercial buildings, and it's worth being precise about why. Applied directly to the interior of roof panels and walls, it delivers roughly R-6.5 per inch, adheres permanently to the steel, seals every lap and fastener penetration as it goes, adds rigidity to the panel system, and — decisive in Kings County — keeps the steel's interior surface warm enough in fog season that condensation never forms. One installed layer does the job of insulation, air barrier, vapor retarder, and acoustic damping. We've been installing it across the South Valley for more than twenty years: family-owned, fully licensed (Lic #C-2-1052735), BBB accredited, SPFA member, and about 35 minutes from Hanford via CA-198. To be clear about our lane: this service is commercial and agricultural buildings only — metal buildings, warehouses, shops, and processing facilities, not houses.

Why Kings County Metal Buildings Bleed Money

A bare or minimally insulated steel building in Hanford loses money four ways at once. The first is radiant heat: a metal roof panel at 150°F on a July afternoon becomes a broiler element aimed at everything below it — inventory, equipment, and people. Buildings with thin vinyl-faced batt sagging between purlins barely blunt this; the steel framing itself bridges heat straight past the batts.

The second is air leakage. Pre-engineered buildings assemble from hundreds of panels and thousands of fasteners, and every lap and screw hole is a small air path. Multiply by a 40-mile-per-hour dust-storm gust and the building breathes hot, dusty outside air all summer — which matters doubly in ag settings where wind-blown grit settles on product, equipment, and anything freshly washed.

The third is condensation, covered fully below. The fourth is comfort-driven behavior: shops that can't be cooled don't run afternoon shifts efficiently, and warehouse pickers slow down measurably in 95°F interiors. Owners tend to discover that the payback calculation on insulation was never really about the PG&E bill alone — it was about the building finally working as designed.

Closed-Cell Foam: What It Does That Nothing Else Does

Not all spray foam is the same product, and for metal buildings the specification matters. We install closed-cell polyurethane foam on steel: roughly R-6.5 per inch, a density near two pounds per cubic foot, and a closed-cell structure that refuses to absorb moisture. Two inches delivers about R-13; three inches about R-19.5 — real, continuous R-value with no gaps, no sag, and no thermal bridging, because the foam covers the purlins and girts as well as the panels.

The properties that matter on Kings County steel, in order: Adhesion — closed-cell foam bonds tenaciously to prepared metal, becoming part of the panel rather than a blanket hung near it; it cannot slump, shift, or be pulled down by vibration, forklifts brushing walls, or decades of thermal cycling. Air sealing — the foam floods every lap, closure, and fastener penetration during application, converting a leaky panel assembly into a sealed envelope in one pass. Vapor control — at two-plus inches, closed-cell foam is its own vapor retarder, which is the technical heart of the condensation fix. Rigidity — foamed panels stiffen noticeably; the oil-canning flex and wind-drumming of big bare panels largely disappears. Open-cell foam, by contrast, is a fine product for the wrong application here — it absorbs moisture and offers half the R-value per inch, and we don't put it on Valley steel.

Condensation and Tule Fog: Ending the Indoor Rain

Ask any Hanford shop owner about winter and you'll hear about the drip. On fog-season nights, bare steel roof panels cool to the fog temperature — often within a few degrees of freezing — while the air inside the building holds moisture from washdowns, stored crops, propane heat, vehicles, or simple occupancy. Where warm moist air meets cold steel, the panel's underside hits dew point and the building rains on itself. Equipment rusts, packaged product gets water-spotted, hay molds, stored paper and cardboard wick, and the slab grows slick patches that are a genuine safety issue.

Closed-cell foam ends this by attacking the physics, not the symptom. With foam bonded to the panel, the steel's interior surface is no longer the cold side of the assembly — the foam face stays near room temperature, safely above dew point, and condensation simply has no cold surface to form on. Because the foam is itself a vapor retarder and air seal, moist interior air can't migrate through to find the cold steel either. This is the single most requested fix we install in Kings County agricultural buildings, and it's binary: buildings that dripped for twenty winters stop dripping the first fog night after application.

Warehouses and Distribution Space Along 198 and 43

Hanford's position — county seat, junction of CA-198 and CA-43, rail-served, midway between the 99 corridor and I-5 — has made it a working distribution node, and distribution buildings have a specific insulation profile. The spaces are tall, the roof area is enormous relative to the walls, and the cooling problem is dominated by the roof deck broiling the top of the racking. Closed-cell foam on the roof panels attacks the problem at its source, cutting radiant load before it enters the space and letting existing HVAC — or big fans alone, in many warehouses — actually hold a workable temperature.

For owners weighing options, the roof question has two good answers and we install both: foam applied to the panel undersides from inside, or an exterior SPF roof system over the panels that insulates and waterproofs simultaneously — the full case for that approach lives on our spray polyurethane foam roofing page. Which one wins depends on the roof's condition, interior access around racking, and whether the panels are due for waterproofing anyway. The free assessment settles it with data rather than preference: drone survey outside, inspection inside, written bid within 48 hours covering the options honestly.

Cold Storage and Processing Facilities

Kings County's ag processing sector — dairy and cheese operations, tomato and vegetable packing, nut handling, and the cold rooms that serve them — runs on refrigeration, and refrigeration economics are insulation economics. Every point of R-value missing from a cold-storage envelope is compressor runtime, purchased daily, forever. Closed-cell foam is the standard envelope upgrade in these facilities for reasons beyond raw R-value: it's seamless (no batt joints for warm moist air to reach the cold side and condense), it's moisture-immune (washdown humidity doesn't degrade it), and it air-seals the thousand penetrations that refrigeration lines, conduit, and equipment mounts punch through processing-building walls.

Processing spaces add their own demands: washdown moisture loads, USDA-adjacent surface expectations in some rooms (foam takes protective coatings where wash-rated surfaces are required), and harvest-calendar scheduling that doesn't pause for contractors. We stage insulation work around production shifts and seasonal windows the same way we stage our roofing work — section by section, coordinated with your operation, no long equipment-down stretches. It's the kind of scheduling fluency that comes from twenty-plus years working ag facilities across the South Valley.

Spray Foam vs. Fiberglass in Metal Buildings

The incumbent comparison is fiberglass — the vinyl-faced batts that came with the building or got draped between purlins later. Here's the honest side-by-side for Kings County steel:

FactorClosed-Cell Spray FoamVinyl-Faced Fiberglass Batts
R-value per inch~R-6.5~R-3 to R-3.5, degraded by compression at framing
Air sealingTotal — floods laps, fasteners, closuresNone — building still breathes dust and heat
Condensation controlBuilt-in vapor retarder; ends panel dripFacing tears leak vapor; batts soak, sag, grow mold
DurabilityBonded to steel; decades, no sagSags, tears at fasteners, degrades in 10–15 years
Moisture behaviorClosed cells absorb essentially noneAbsorbs washdown/fog moisture, loses R-value wet
Structural effectStiffens panels, damps wind drummingNone
Installed costHigher upfront per square footCheaper upfront, replaced repeatedly

Fiberglass wins exactly one row of that table — first cost — and loses the rest, most decisively in the rows Kings County cares about: air sealing against dust, condensation control against fog, and moisture behavior in washdown environments. The wet-batt problem deserves emphasis: fiberglass that has absorbed a few fog seasons of condensation isn't insulation anymore, it's a damp blanket holding moisture against your steel. A significant share of our commercial insulation projects in Hanford begin by removing exactly that.

What Commercial Spray Foam Insulation Costs

Spray foam insulation cost per square foot for commercial metal-building work depends on thickness, prep, and access, and honest context beats a teaser number. The variables: specified depth (two inches of closed-cell costs less than three; R-targets drive depth), substrate condition (clean newer panels spray fast; older buildings may need washing, rust treatment, or old batt removal first), interior access (open shell versus working around racking, lines, and equipment), and total area (mobilization spreads thinner across bigger jobs — and Kings County buildings tend to be big, which works in your favor).

Rather than publish a number that's wrong in both directions, we do it the accurate way: free on-site assessment, measured areas, verified substrate condition, and a written bid within 48 hours with the R-value math shown. If the smarter money for your building is an exterior SPF roof system instead of interior insulation, the bid will say that too, with the roofing economics laid out the same way they are on our spray foam roofing cost page. What we can promise up front: the energy delta on an un-insulated steel building in this climate is large enough that insulation is one of the few building upgrades with a genuine, calculable payback period.

Title 24, R-Values, and the Energy Math

California's Title 24 energy code applies to commercial alterations and additions, not just new construction, and insulation levels are core to it. Closed-cell foam's arithmetic makes compliance straightforward: R-13 at two inches, R-19.5 at three, installed continuously — and "continuously" is the word that matters, because code-referenced performance assumes insulation actually covering the assembly rather than batts compressed to nothing at every purlin. On alteration projects in Hanford, foam frequently lets an existing steel building meet envelope requirements without framing modifications.

The operating math is more persuasive than the code math. Take a 20,000-square-foot bare-steel warehouse in Hanford: summer roof panels at 150°F radiating downward, cooling equipment fighting a losing battle, PG&E commercial rates doing the scoring. Three inches of closed-cell foam changes the roof from a broiler element into an R-19.5 barrier and simultaneously seals the air leakage that was importing 105°F outside air. Owners see it in the first summer bill; facility managers see it in equipment runtime; crews feel it by the first week of July. Fog-season heating tells the same story in reverse — the foam that stops condensation also stops the steel from stripping heat out of the space on 35°F mornings.

Roof-Side and Wall-Side: The Whole-Envelope Approach

Because we're a roofing company and an insulation company in one shop, we can treat a steel building as a single envelope instead of two trades' territories. The strongest configuration for many Kings County buildings pairs an exterior SPF roof — waterproofing and R-value over the panels, installed per our spray foam roofing installation process — with interior closed-cell foam on the walls. Roof-side application solves waterproofing, fastener leaks, and the radiant load in one system; wall-side application seals the remaining air paths and finishes the thermal boundary. Buildings that get both stop being metal boxes with weather inside them and start behaving like conditioned space.

Sequencing is flexible and budget-respecting: plenty of Hanford owners do the roof one year and the walls the next, or foam the cold-storage rooms first and the shop later. The assessment maps the whole envelope and prices the phases separately, so the plan matches your capital cycle rather than a contractor's ideal invoice.

How Installation Works in an Occupied Building

Commercial insulation installs happen in working buildings, and our process is built around that reality. Preparation comes first: surfaces cleaned, old failed batts removed where present (their disposal handled properly), rust treated, and everything that shouldn't get foam on it — equipment, lines, product, finished surfaces — masked and protected with the same discipline we bring to spraying near neighboring property on downtown roofs. Application proceeds in controlled passes to the specified depth, area by area, with your operation's schedule dictating the sequence; overnight and weekend windows are routine for us in processing facilities. Ventilation is managed during and after application per the material's re-occupancy specifications, and we verify installed depth as we go rather than estimating it afterward.

You get documentation at the end — areas covered, depths installed, R-values achieved — because insulation you can't prove might as well not exist when the building sells, the Title 24 paperwork comes due, or the refrigeration contractor asks what the envelope is doing. It's the same documentation habit that runs through everything we install, backed by industry-leading leak-proof guarantees on the roofing side of the house.

Will spray foam stop my metal building from dripping inside during tule fog season?

Yes — and it's the most common reason Kings County owners call us. Fog-season drip is condensation: warm moist interior air meeting steel panels chilled to fog temperature. Closed-cell foam bonded to the panels keeps the interior surface above dew point and acts as its own vapor retarder, so the condensation physically can't form. Buildings that dripped for twenty winters stop the first fog night after application.

Closed-cell foam delivers roughly R-6.5 per inch, installed continuously over panels, purlins, and girts — so about R-13 at two inches and R-19.5 at three, with none of the compression losses that gut fiberglass batts at every framing member. Is spray foam really better than the fiberglass batts that came with my building?

For Valley steel, decisively.
